# Copper February 2011 

- As we noted in our last report, what did indeed turn out to be the January month low copper cash price on the 25th of US$9330/t ($4.23/lb) now seems to be far away, as the red metal surged upward for the following nine consecutive trading days to hit a fresh record high. 

- Our overall market balances for 2011 and 2012 have firmed a little since last month’s report and hence our price forecasts have edged up slightly, accordingly.  By the time we see fresh metal demand from China, we anticipate that the upstream mining issues will be fully coming into play and will contribute to the near 400kt metal deficit we show for the second quarter alone.  Given that we do not anticipate any respite from this side of the market through to the end of year, we expect cash quotes to surge past recent records, leaving us with an average of US$10,000/t ($4.54/lb) for the second half of this year. 

- The broad themes impacting demand from last month continued through February, with Europe steady, China in a holiday lull and US markets in a tentative recovery.  With the Chinese year of the rabbit now upon us, many will be hoping for Chinese demand to be quickly out of the trap, although we expect solid if not spectacular growth in Chinese refined consumption this year.  For Europe and the US the pace of activity is more likely to resemble a tortoise, however, in line with our slow but steady consumption growth forecasts. 

- There has been considerable progress in the long-term concentrate market over the past month, with many deals having been concluded between miners and smelting companies at the $56/t & 5.6c/lb benchmark established by Freeport earlier this year.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Technical trading pushes copper to new highs in early February…** As we noted in our last report, what did indeed turn out to be the January month low copper cash price on the 25<sup>th</sup> of US$9330/t ($4.23/lb) now seems to be so far away, as the red metal surged upward for the following nine consecutive trading days to US$10,145/t ($4.60/lb – cash) through to February 7<sup>th</sup> .  Aided by a healthy collection of supply-side

outages and other physicals concerns during the final week of January and into early February, the main price driver was more so the technicals behind squaring off positions ahead of the Chinese New Year holidays, which began on the 3<sup>rd</sup> .  Monetary tightening measures by the Chinese government - and the prospect of more - prompted a temporary increase in the local margin requirements for the holiday period duration from the usual 11% to 20%, and closing out of some Shanghai-LME arbitrage positions pushed short-covering higher.  Consequently, the LME moved higher also, and the arb narrowed from c.$400/t on the 28<sup>th</sup> January to c.$310/t by February 1<sup>st</sup> .  But this was, as we say, a temporary shift driven by abnormal circumstances, and once trading recommenced on the 9<sup>th</sup> , the arb moved further out to c.$360/t.  Interestingly, although the SHFE-LME differential has moved quite erratically since then, the general trend has brought the two prices closer together, with c.$220/t being the average since mid-month. 

**..followed by a lull** Most market commentators, including ourselves, had expected a run-up in copper prices ahead of the Chinese holiday period, then a lull for the six-day duration, and then a virtual resumption of the surge, given that the Chinese would be back in the market.  However, rarely are expectations matched, and these were no exceptions.  The LME edged up by c.US$300/t with the Chinese away, to that US$10,145/t level on the 7<sup>th</sup> , then fell back US$215/t in anticipation of their return.  LME cash moved to a low for that week of US$9,875/t ($4.48/lb) on the 10<sup>th</sup> , and that floor was sufficient to bring buyers back to the market looking for fresh gains.  Opening on Monday 14<sup>th</sup> indeed did see a new record price - $3/t up on the 7<sup>th</sup> – but this has proved to be too rich for most, particularly in light of the growing unrest in northern Africa and the Middle East and prices melted away below US$9800/t by the 18<sup>th</sup> .  The fact that they have since only edged up and yet stayed well below the US$9850/t mark indicates that the market is in need of a rationale for fresh direction, and there are indeed as many reasons to believe prices will go higher as there are to go lower. 

**Supply-side issues contribute to price push…** As we noted above, there were some supplier issues during that lateJanuary, early February period which increased concern over new metal reaching the market and stoked the discussion over ongoing near-term tightness.  Most of these were in the market already, but the rash of 2010 year-end results published by several producers renewed the focus on lower output generally.  The minor drop in refined metal from Chile last year (from 3.272Mt in 2009 to 3.24Mt) was no surprise, as was Norilsk’s final 389kt _vs._ its prior guidance of 393398kt.  But a plant shutdown at Vedanta Resources’ KCM smelter in Zambia (January 28<sup>th</s

up> ) and the explosion at Xstrata’s Kristiansand copper section in Norway (Feb 4th ) will add to the losses in the near term in which we are already forecasting a net metal market deficit of c.400kt through to June, increasing to 585kt by the year’s end. Aside from these producers with unexpected outages, the market nervously watched the cyclone pass through northern Queensland which brought a halt to normal operations at several mining and metallurgical complexes, including Xstrata’s 300kt/a Townsville copper refinery and Kagara Zinc’s mines. Other, previously advertised shortfalls in intermediates output anticipated for the middle of this year will be coming from Chile’s Escondida, Grasberg and Batu Hijau in Indonesia and Bingham Canyon in the USA, all for declining grade issues as they transition through to higher grade sequencing in their pits from 2012-2013. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 12000

There is no doubt that this period of near-$10,000/t price levels for copper has had an effect on the extent to its use, with overall demand dropping away at a rate of 2% per year (see our _Insight_ on this very subject from earlier this month). But several suppliers of copper products believe that the easy areas for substitution have been made already, and that the focus among top tier semis suppliers in Western World countries at any rate lies at the higher end applications if they expect to survive. Even so, with either a deficit or relative tightness in the metal markets built into our analysis through to mid-2012, we can expect further loss in the lower end of copper’s use, with roofing a real candidate to die away altogether, along with various applications in transport and the low/high voltage markets. However, perhaps more importantly, it was apparent to us at the North American Food Equipment Suppliers meeting in Orlando, FL earlier this month that heat exchange tubing has not escaped such attention in the US/Canada. Typically made from copper, several users are now asking manufacturers to consider using aluminium, and painted carbon steel versions are already being made in South Korea. **High metal prices do not necessarily mean low demand…** In the face of all these bearish overtones, though, it is apparent from our discussions with semis producers in Europe and the USA (although not China) that demand for their products, from wire rod to tube, is high and rising – back, even, to pre-crisis levels in some areas. Clearly, these producers are managing to avoid the sectors such as construction and certain low-end automotive wire and power cables markets where business activity remains weak. With China’s copper needs having been largely directed to these areas, the mediocre copper demand levels there are self-explanatory. High-performance automotive parts and electronics and superfine wire demand are driving forces behind the strong copper uptake currently outside China, and at least one German-based wire rod manufacturer will be adding another shift to its workforce in early March to step up production rates as a result of stronger orders this month. **..but financing the metal does bring its challenges** But not all players are well-placed to benefit from these dynamics. Clearly reacting to US$10,000/t copper prices, Swedish wire rod supplier Elektrokoppar was quoted this month as saying that “it cannot act as “bankers” to its customers any longer,” and it has shortened payment terms to its customers by half. Furthermore, it will cut out the fourth shift at its principal rod mill and reduce output of low-end rod products by 20% from the end of this month. It may be, then, that when one fabricator reports strong business, he is merely picking up orders that are left unsatisfied from another. But the implications are that the _nature_ of the copper semis business is changing in what would typically be called “high-cost” countries, and this will force the players involved to change their ways if they are to survive. Further down the processing chain, the USA’s Southwire closed two building products-related wire plants at Kingman, AZ and Watkinsville, GA at the end of 2010, as planned back in May last year, so that higher capacity utilisation rates could be achieved at other in-house facilities. **Scrap is filling the void, though, rather than primary metal** Despite these reports of strong refined copper offtake in Europe and the USA mainly, though, it is not primary cathode producers who are seeing the benefit. Secondary smelters and r

efiners are overflowing with scrap and have been since last September in Europe and the summer months in the USA. With copper prices likely to remain high through to the summer at least, it is likely that obsolete scrap will continue to be collected in the hefty quantities that we have seen for most of the past year, and now that industrial activity is also picking up in the main geographic consuming regions, we will see prompt industrial scrap levels also rising. In theory, scrap discounts even on No.2 qualities in Europe could have gone as high as €500/t by now, but as all the plants are full Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2011 Page 3 of 23 Copper Monthly Update and as there is little buying activity taking place, a more representative figure in the spot market is closer to €200-300/t, although one player is known to be testing the €420-450/t mark even now. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 10

**Cathode premia soften in the USA and China** High scrap availability has taken its toll on the cathode market, though. In the US, we believe cathode sales are reportedly pretty soft and have been since the start of this year, and Midwest premia on cathode have fallen from last month’s 5.0-5.5c/lb to 4.5-5.5c/lb during February. Meanwhile, the holidays in China and the relatively low level of buying interest since then have conspired to depress imported cathode premia to c.$20/t from the $30-70/t range of a month ago. Meanwhile, domestic cathode sales are running at a discount in RMB terms _vs._ the SHFE price, and the probability of February industrial activity being fairly low due to the holidays is unlikely to have brought any change to these terms. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Copper Monthly Update 

**Warehouse cathode stocks surge** With the preference being for secondary metal where applicable, primary cathode has been heading for exchange warehouses at a consistent rate.  For the third straight month, LME copper stocks ended up in January at 394kt, from end-November’s 355kt.  By February 23<sup>rd</sup> , this figure had once again moved up to 412.7t, but it is noticeable that the increase has all come from within Asian destinations, in particular South Korea.  While European stock locations have dropped by a net 6kt or so, and the US equally held 2.9kt less, Korean LME stocks have risen by c.19.5kt, with the most likely explanations being that this represents either material that was already in Chinese bonded warehouses being re-exported, or metal that was headed for China and was diverted to Korean ports instead. 

In the USA, metal has moved into Comex during February, with total stocks rising by almost 15% since the end of January to reach 81.2kt (short) by the 23<sup>rd</sup> .  Salt Lake and Toledo have been the principal recipients (up by 5.2kst and 4kst, to 12.85kst and 9.9kst, respectively), while the main depots of El Paso (29.3kst) and Tucson (28.1 kst) received only a net additional 600st each over the period. Meanwhile, as a reflection of the poor market in China, SHFE stocks have continued their surge to reach 161kt by February 18<sup>th</sup> , up from a recent low of 129.3kt on January 28<sup>th</sup> . 

**Near-term outlook bearish for prices…** Weighing up current market conditions, we see LME prices continuing to be quite hesitant about moves closer to the previous highs of US$10,000/t, and instead edging back down to trade within the reasonably narrow range of US$9,450-9650/t ($4.29-4.38/lb) through to the end of March.  The $300/t increase to our Q1 price forecast, which now stands at an average of US$9,650/t ($4.38/lb), reflects the price strength seen into February.  Somewhat clouding the picture is the ongoing unrest in northern African and Middle Eastern countries that has forced many market participants to become more risk averse, in so doing dragging down prices throughout the base metals complex.  However, although high copper prices will deter Chinese (or for that matter any) fabricators from holding anything other than minimal cathode inventories, having spent the last five months or so running down their product stocks, it is now only a matter of time before an uptick in consumer buying leads to a reversal in the market’s fortunes.  And, even if much of this fresh demand is initially satisfied

by the current glut of metal held in bonded warehouses, any news of rising consumption in the world’s largest copper consuming economy is likely to provide the next kick-start for copper prices in the immediate term. 

**..but we expect prices to pick up by early Q2** Our overall market balances for 2011 and 2012 have firmed a little since last month’s report and hence our price forecasts have edged up slightly, accordingly.  By the time we see fresh metal demand from China, we anticipate that the upstream mining issues will be fully coming into play and will contribute to the near 400kt metal deficit we show for the second quarter alone.  Given that we do not anticipate any respite from this side of the market through to the end of year, we expect cash quotes to surge past recent records, leaving us with an average of US$10,000/t ($4.54/lb) for the second half of this year.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

The broad themes impacting demand from last month continued through February, with Europe steady, China in a holiday lull and US markets in a tentative recovery.  With the Chinese year of the rabbit now upon us, many will be hoping for Chinese demand to be quickly out of the trap, although we expect solid if not spectacular growth in Chinese refined consumption this year.  For Europe and the US the pace of activity is more likely to resemble a tortoise, however, in line with our slow but steady consumption growth forecasts. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Cold snap leads to economic slip…** Euro zone industrial output slipped marginally in December, as severe winter weather impeded activity in Germany in particular.  On the same month a year ago, however, output was up by 8.2%, while fourth quarter growth was up by a solid 1.6% from Q3.  Industrial orders data suggests that the European recovery continues to be driven by manufacturing and indeed, this has translated into the current steady growth in demand for copper.  New industrial orders in the euro zone were up by 19.9% y-o-y in November, with strong growth in capital goods.  Consumer durables, on the other hand, were weak.  Together with the ongoing improvement in euro zone PMIs, the data points to continued growth in European IP through the first quarter, which will be sustain momentum in refined consumption.  However, the recovery is not yet broad based, geographically or sectorally, which raises uncertainty over the sustainability of the recovery later in the year. 

**…but consumer sentiment thaws a little** There are a few positive signs for underlying economic consumption in Europe.  EZ consumer confidence rose to its highest level since end 2007 in February, with reduced fear of job losses boosting sentiment.  At -9.9, the survey balance shows more consumers are negative on the outlook than positive, but the series has been below zero since 2001 and continued improvement in the indicator should be viewe

d with optimism. **Semis producers warming to improved order levels** Despite the mixed economic picture, discussions with market participants reveal that most players are satisfied with their order intake and that semis output at this very early stage in the year is at least keeping pace with 2010 and in many cases is ahead of it. This is the case across the range of products, including wire rod and brass mill products such as strip. Meanwhile, Aurubis have released their latest quarterly production data, which revealed a 14.5% year on year increase in wire rod output to 198kt in the October to December quarter of 2010, while cast shape output was 8% higher on the prior year at 54kt. For the full calendar year wire rod output was up by 24.4% on 2009 at 791kt, while cast shape output surged by 39% to 214kt. These figures do indeed represent very strong growth, although wire rod sales in particular is likely to have been aided by the closure of Nexans’ Chauny wire rod plant in France in early 2010. As such, the increase in output at Aurubis is ahead of our estimate of Western European refined demand growth in 2010 of 13.3%. #### **Aurubis copper wire rod production – (kt)** 120 240

However, there seems to be much more going

on in the European market place than headline European numbers viewed in isolation would suggest.  For instance, Sweden’s Elektrokoppar recently revealed that they are cutting a production shift and in doing so reducing output of wire rod by around 20%.  They cite the high copper price as behind the reduction, which was accompanied by shortening payment terms of their customers.  Clearly, a higher copper price increases working capital requirements for firms because of a higher cost of their own inventory and as explicitly stated by financing consumer’s purchases through payment terms.  We have noted some firms picking up orders for prompt delivery, which may not be as a result of Elektrokoppar cutting production but perhaps is in line with our reports last month that Kovohuty’s wire rod line in Slovakia may be off line at the moment. 

**Euro zone car sales in reverse** New car registrations fell by 1.1% in January to 1.07M vehicles, the third consecutive monthly fall, and reinforcing the view that new car purchases are likely to be lacklustre in 2011.  Auto makers will continue to pin their hopes on the export market for growth, although the production picture is distinctly mixed.  German

car production in January was up by 10.4% year on year, while UK vehicle output increased by 8.9%.  However, Italian car output fell 17% in December, and Spain’s dipped 3%.  Although on the face of it this overall sluggish tone to the European car market should point to weakness in copper demand from the sector although it is worth remembering that the average German car typically has more copper content than most other countries because of the number of premium car marques that are produced in the country.  As such, if there is one European car producing country that copper semis producers would want to be performing reasonably well above any other it would be Germany. 

**Cracks remain in construction sector** The construction sector continues to represent the weak spot for demand, with general cable orders lagging other key sectors.  Although there are some signs of life in residential building in parts of Europe, increased fiscal restraint will act to offset this to leave construction demand anemic overall.  Electrical and electronic products are faring better though, supported by continued localisation of power distribution and modest improvement in demand for consumer electronics. 

**Higher starting point for 2011 demand** As a result of more up to date data becoming available we have increased our estimate of Western European refined demand in 2010, which has resulted in our 2011 number having a higher starting point.  We now forecast 1.9% growth in Western European demand this year, following an estimated 13.3% expansion in 2010. 

### **Americas** 

**The US economic outlook has improved considerably…** At the start of the year, Wood Mackenzie upgraded

its forecast for 2011 US GDP growth from 1.8% to 3.1% (see the Insight 2011 – The Year of Reckoning), reflecting the impact of further fiscal and monetary stimulus measures announced by authorities in late 2010.  In our view, these are sufficient boosts to inject the US economy with enough momentum to transition from stimulus and inventory driven recovery into self-sustaining growth. 

**..with the focus being on consumer spending** Recent data suggest that households are now showing an increased appetite for spending, releasing some of their pent up demand, and the pay-roll tax breaks should lend further impetus to domestic demand this year.  US domestic consumption gained momentum through late 2010.  Retail sales improved steadily through the quarter, with autos in particular seeing strong growth.  Q4 GDP data for the US showed real final sales (which omit inventory changes) expanded at an annualised rate of 7.1%, the fastest growth in more than four years and providing a solid boost to wider economic growth.  The most recent indicators suggest that such growth may continue through the first half of 2011 - the Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index reached a three-year high of 70.4 in February, coming in well above market expectations (although confidence remains well below the level of 2004 to 2007. 

**However, structural problems remain** High unemployment, a blighted housing market and high indebtedness of households are still the chief concerns.  While unemployment has fallen in the past couple of months, from 9.8% in November to 9% in January, it has remained stubbornly high.  This has been the result of people leaving the labour force as much as job creation.  In practice, firms appear to have reached the end of their lay-off rounds some months ago, and this likely contributed to the improved consumer spending, but new job creation has been distinctly lacking.  The disappointing labour market data so far suggests that most of the employment gains have been driven by a recovery in the average hourly workweek (firms asking workers to resume full time hours), rather than new hiring by firms.  That said, there are some pockets of strength: manufacturing payrolls jumped in January, and the manufacturing PMI indicated that sector employers are looking to expand hiring at the fastest rate since the 1970s.  But the manufacturing sector only accounts for 25% or so of the US economy, leaving the weaker sectors still taking their toll on any wider jobs recovery. 

**Slight improvement in metal demand…** In copper terms, this general improvement in the US economy has translated into slightly stronger metal demand than we initially thought.  Despite the tail-off in wire rod and brass mill production in the final quarter of last year, we estimate that 2010 copper demand will have improved by 6.7% on 2009, although we should remind ourselves that 2009 consumption did witness a near 18.5% collapse on the prior year.  Even so, at 1.76Mt for 2010, cop

per demand remains back at 1983 levels, and so the use of the word “recovery” has to be somewhat kept in perspective. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - February 2011 Page 8 of 23 Copper Monthly Update #### **US brass mill shipments – (kt)** 20 100

**...but sectoral contraction will remain a feature in the processing business** Despite these encouraging signs for manufacturing, the ongoing contraction in the copper wire and cable sector (including some outright plant closures contained within planned corporate M&As) points to the challenges being faced by the processing segment of the copper business. Southwire, for example, closed two wire plants at the end of 2010 as planned back in April 2010 following two significant and separate acquisitions earlier that year, and it will bring wire production from those plants into its main Carrollton facility in Georgia to enhance its downstream utilisation rate. The two facilities that are now closed used to make residential and commercial building wire, and the rationale for this contraction – and further closures across the sector - remains strong. The knock-on effect of such contraction, though, for upstream wire rod suppliers is that Southwire will no doubt look to supply their newly-owned wire-making plants with its own rod out of Carrollton, leaving previous rod suppliers looking for other outlets to take up the slack if they are to avoid closure themselves. #### **US copper wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

**Minimal demand growth expected** This year, refined metal demand in the USA for cathode via the primary route has been lukewarm at best as the secondary sector has benefited from ample material at favourable market terms – as has been the case in other regions. We have already seen cathode stocks rise (principally in Comex warehouses), with metal from Kennecott’s Garfield held at the Salt Lake depot increasing substantially during February and southwestern producers adding to Tucson and El Paso. With this outlook, it is fortunate that refined production in the US will be somewhat constrained this year, with Garfield’s near 50kt anticipated drop largely countering small increments elsewhere. But our minimal demand increase of just 20kt for this year to 1.78Mt reflects our conservative view that while Metals

### **China** 

**Price pressures raise the prospect of further rate hikes** The Chinese New Year has resulted in a paucity of economic data releases this month, while there was little to be surprised about in data that was released.  Starting with prices, inflation reached 4.9% in January, up from 4.6% in December and is clearly more than simply a food issue, as non-food inflation was at its highest since 2005.  Inflation in China is not in itself a cause for concern, if higher wage growth provides a boost to consumption.  What has observers worried is the reaction of the authorities and the potential impact on industry. 

In response to mounting inflationary pressures, China hiked interest rates on February 8th for the third time since October, taking the lending rate to 6.06% and the deposit rate to 3%.  Reserve ratio requirements, which effectively limit money supply, were also raised, for the eighth time, taking the RRR to 20%.  The new loans data for January suggest liquidity remains ample and that further increases in rates are likely, although anecdotal evidence does point to credit conditions at least beginning to tighten. 

**Plenty of celebratory fireworks but February demand lacked sparkle** As expected, demand for refined metal has been sluggish in February, with China on holiday for New Year celebrations.  Most semis producers were off for the full week long holiday this year, compared to the average 2-3 days in 2010, although fabricators remain confident on the short term outlook and have reasonably full order books.  However, a combination of high metal prices and tightening credit conditions has made inventories increasingly difficult to finance and producers are unwilling to increase stocks above current low levels.  In addition, end users are pushing back on price increases and this is squeezing margins. Given the rumoured rising levels of refined copper in bonded warehouses even if fabricators did choose to increase stocks this would not immediately be reflected in improved apparent consumption calculations in any case. 

**Authorities clamp down further on real estate speculation…** In the construction sector, housing policy tightening measures in Beijing have been introduced, requiring non-residents to provide five years of tax revenues in order to buy a house, and banning residents from buying a third home.  Some estimates suggest that sales could fall by as much as 30% as a result of this.  With other cities also introducing restrictions, Dragonomics estimates sales nationwide could dip 10% this year.  A collapse in building remains a key risk to the economy in 2011, although the expansion of low cost housing does perhaps provide something of an insurance

policy for both the sector and the wider economy. **…but car sales stay in the fast lane** Flying in the face of an expected slowdown, vehicle sales in China in January hit a record high of 1.8944 million units, an increase of 13.8% y-o-y, according to provisional data. Subsidy expiration does not appear to have hit sales yet. Production of vehicles totalled 1.80 million units, an 11.3% y-o-y increase, but down by 3.6% from December’s record high. **Refined estimate for 2011 demand** In line with an abundance of scrap in the Chinese market, we have lowered our refined demand forecast for 2011 to 6% growth from 7% previously, although we have kept our total copper growth number in tact at 10%. China continues to invest in scrap processing and this will temper refined demand growth this year. **China’s January concentrate imports down by 4.3% on a year earlier** In January 2011 China’s copper concentrate imports were 571Mdmt which was 4.3% lower than in the same period last year.  That said on an annualised basis the January imports were running almost 6% higher than the 2010 monthly average.  The combined contributions from Chile, Peru, and Mexico accounted for just over 50% of these receipts, with Australia, the US and Mongolia also featuring as significant suppliers.  Perhaps the most significant news in the Chinese market this month was the re

-start of Yunnan’s smelting operations in Kunming on February 20<sup>th</sup> .  The company closed its IsaSmelt furnace and ancillary equipment for an extensive maintenance and overhaul programme that was due to take two hundred and seventy five days.  The sheer length of this closure led some commentators to question whether the outage could have been driven as much by unfavourable market conditions (i.e. low international TC/RCs and high inland freight costs).  In the event, the operation reopened forty one days ahead of schedule.  During the shutdown the Kunming tankhouse was supplied with blister and anodes from local smelters in Yunnan province and also from the company’s part-owned 150kt/a Chambishi smelter in Zambia.  The Kunming smelter has the capacity to produce 200kt/a of copper anodes from primary sources and from purchased secondaries and Yunnan Copper typically buys 750kt/a of concentrates from the international market. 

**Tough times ahead for traders** After several years of buoyant market conditions many traders are now facing much tougher times.  This in part reflects earlier spot purchases that have left buyers long of expensive concentrates that are presently out of the money.  In addition, TC/RCs in a significant number of traders’ long-term contracts are established in relation to benchmark numbers.  This means that trader deals with miners are being referenced to recent long-term settlements at the $56/t & 5.6c/lb mark while various buyers, most notably in Asia are referencing long-term deals of between $65/t & 6.5c/lb and $70/t & 7c/lb, potentially leaving traders with a buy/sell differential of $14/t & 1.4c/lb instead of the more usual $5-10/t & 0.5-1.0c/lb gap. 

**Oyu Tolgoi concentrates up for sale** Traders have also been active in North America of late on account of Freeport apparently being long of material in Arizona due to the ramp up of the Morenci mine.  It appears that Freeport has invited merchants to bid for these surplus concentrates on a multi-year basis.  According to our estimates, unless the Miami smelter is expanded, the excess is set to increase further beyond 2012 with the re-start of the Chino mill in New Mexico. Elsewhere, Rio Tinto is rumoured to have invited traders to participate in acquiring a proportion of the projected output from its Oyu Tolgoi mine in Mongolia.  The mine is due to start up in 2013 with production rising in successive years to 2.3Mdmt/a of concentrates by 2020.  Thus far, the owners have already received expressions of interest to purchase at least 500kt/a of concentrates from Chinese smelters including Jiangxi Copper, Jinlong, Jinchuan and Tongling.

**Chilean refined metal production slips by 1% in 2010…** According to data from Cochilco in Chile, national refined metal output slipped by 1% last year on 2009 to 3.24Mt, with the most notable declines being at the Chuquicamata complex (down a total 20kt to 660kt), El Abra (down 19kt on 2009 to c.145kt), Escondida (-27kt to 300kt), and Gaby (- 30kt to 117kt). **…and Codelco’s output falls by a similar amount** Of that 3.24Mt nationwide tally, Codelco’s operations accounted for c.1.76Mt, _vs._ 1.782Mt in 2009 (including its 49% stake in El Abra). Now that Gaby has worked through some technical issues associated with its expansion programme and secured a new labour agreement, we forecast SxEw output there to rise to 160kt this year, topping out at 165kt for the following two-year period.  Meanwhile Andina, which has also been undergoing expansion work should return to its former glories this year, producing c.260kt of copper contained in concentrate and putting it on a par with levels last seen between 1999-2001.  As we noted in our January report, Codelco expects to produce 1.8Mt of commercial copper in 2011, which will represent a recent high, but this largely reflects a return to “normal business” rather than by dint of specific investment programmes that will come to fruition over the course of this year.  Start-up at the Ministro Hales (formerly Mansa Mina) mine is likely to come only by late 2013, building to c.200kt/a metal contained in concentrate, while further expansion studies ongoing at Andina will not bear fruit until later this decade, when an additional 300kt/a copper in concentrate could arise from 2018.

**Kazakhstan output expected to rise this year** Glencore-controlled Kazzinc produced its first 30t of electrolytically refined cathode at Ust-Kamenogorsk in December, and we anticipate 35kt from this plant this year, building to 70kt/a over the following two years.  Previously, the company said that cathode would become available from March this year, and so it could be that this initial cathode came as a result of purchased anode being trialled through the tankhouse. This is the first cathode to come from Kazzinc; last year’s output of c.50kt copper in concentrate from its Zyrianovsk and Ridder complexes was c.16% down on the prior year’s 59.kt.  One of the country’s largest producer, Kazakhmys, produced slightly less copper in 2010 at 303.3kt from its four complexes (down from 320kt in 2009), and although it has several investment plans ongoing, output is projected to remain level through to at least 2014, after which the company expects to bring its Aktogay and Boschekul mine-concentrator projects on line at an cost of $2Bn each with both facilities expected to produce 100kt/a metal contained.
